tip: The -इए (-iye) ending marks a polite command: बंद कर दीजिए (band kar dijiye) is for people you call आप (aap) – with friends it drops to बंद कर दो (band kar do).
बंद कर दो (band kar do) – the added दो (do = give) marks the action as done for someone else. Plain बंद करो (band karo) is the bare order; कर दो adds 'for me'.
A helper लो (lo, from लेना = take) marks the action as for your own benefit: छाता साथ ले लो (chhata saath le lo) = take the umbrella along, for yourself. Acting for others uses दो (do) instead.
Commands say no with मत (mat), not नहीं (nahin): ऐसा मत करो (aisa mat karo = don't do that). नहीं belongs to statements; मत is the don't-word.
A command for later uses the -ना form: दवाई समय पर लेना (davai samay par lena) = take your medicine when the time comes. लो (lo) would mean do it right now.
ज़रा (zara = just a little) softens a command the way English 'just' does: ज़रा एक टैक्सी बुक कर दो (zara ek taxi book kar do) sounds friendly, not bossy.
तैयार हो जा (taiyar ho ja) uses the bare stem – the तू (tu) command kept for kids and very close friends. With anyone else it sounds harsh: use हो जाओ (ho jao).
For states, Hindi commands the change with हो जाना (ho jana = become): शांत हो जाइए (shaant ho jaiye) is literally 'become quiet', not 'be quiet'.
Hindi chains steps with -कर (-kar = having done): हाथ धोकर खाना खाओ (haath dhokar khana khao) = 'having washed hands, eat'. One sentence, no 'and then'.
करना (karna) has an irregular polite command – कीजिए (kijiye), not kariye: मदद कीजिए (madad kijiye = please help). देना and लेना match: दीजिए (dijiye), लीजिए (lijiye).
A final ना (na) turns an order into coaxing: चाय बना दो ना (chai bana do na) = 'come on, make some tea, won't you'. Here ना pleads – it doesn't negate.
रहिए (rahiye) after बैठे keeps a state going: बैठे रहिए (baithe rahiye) = remain seated. बैठिए (baithiye) alone would invite them to sit down.
करा (kara) means someone else does it: पासबुक अपडेट करा लो (passbook update kara lo) = get it updated – the clerk does the work, not you.
Relaying an order: नरेश से कहिए कि (Naresh se kahiye ki = tell Naresh that) + आ जाए (aa jae = he should come). The relayed verb shifts to the should-form, not आओ (aao).
भैया (bhaiya = brother) is the normal way to address a shopkeeper you don't know – Hindi uses family words for friendly strangers, so no name needed.
Being heard is phrased with देना (dena = give): सुनाई नहीं दे रहा (sunai nahin de raha) = literally 'not giving to hearing' = can't be heard. Seeing works the same: दिखाई देना (dikhai dena).
चलो (chalo = let's go) opens a 'let's' suggestion, then the verb stays plain: ताज़ी हवा लेते हैं (taazi hawa lete hain) = 'we take fresh air', meaning let's.
जी (ji) after a name adds respect: सुनील जी (Sunil ji) is like 'Mr Sunil' but warmer – used for elders, customers, anyone you'd call आप (aap).
